Using power responsibly

Who decides what matters?

A score can change when we change what matters most.

A closer lookOpen the shared interactive reader ↗

The interactive example has its own motion control. Scroll inside it if you need more room.

Results in an invented model; real-world testing is still needed

Imagine two plans. In this made-up example, A scores 8 for speed and 2 for thoroughness. B has the opposite scores. Move the slider to change how much speed should count.

The options stay the same while their ranking changes. The numbers are invented and describe no people. The example makes one question visible: who chose what the score should value?

Move the slider to change what the score values. The options themselves stay the same.

Words used here
weight
How much a quantity contributes to a combined score.
tradeoff
Gaining something while giving up something else.
Read the fuller explanation

Two toy options sit on this desk. One has more of the first quantity and less of the second; the other reverses that arrangement. Move the declared weight and watch the arithmetic ranking change. Neither option has changed its two coordinates.

These numbers are invented for the illustration and describe no people, outcomes or source dataset. Their role is to make aggregation inspectable. In the older Worldwright model, the landscape likewise distinguishes a diagnostic aggregate from moral or political authority.

A responsible account names its objective, whose judgment supplied it and which costs the score can conceal. It can also retain the alternatives when there is no agreed single ranking.

Where this comes from: Results from an invented social model

Results in an invented model; real-world testing is still needed

The reported ranking changes with urgency and with the chosen score. The model has not been shown to predict real communities or decide what is morally right.

Worldwright research: current landscape

The older research model is distinct from this storytelling product. Its frozen cells expose urgency-dependent aggregate rankings and Pareto tradeoffs under declared assumptions. Its mechanisms remain empirically unidentified; no policy, personal advice or moral authority follows from the rankings.
